summary.text: The geometric sum for a nontrivial thirteenth root of unity, rewritten using \(\zeta+\zeta^{-1}=2\cos\theta\), yields a degree-six cosine polynomial; the double-angle identity then shows that each \(4\cos^2(\pi k/13)\) satisfies the corresponding reciprocal denominator equation. These six values are positive and distinct by the strict behavior of cosine on \([0,\pi]\), so the six resulting roots determine the monic degree-six polynomial, with its constant term fixing the normalization of the product.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(x)=1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6.
\]
We prove that
\[
P(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right).
\]
The argument begins by obtaining a polynomial satisfied by the relevant cosine values from the thirteenth roots of unity.

Define
\[
g(y)=y^6+y^5-5y^4-4y^3+6y^2+3y-1.
\]
We first show that, for every integer \(n\) with \(1\le n\le 12\),
\[
g\left(2\cos\frac{2\pi n}{13}\right)=0. \tag{1}
\]
Fix such an \(n\), put
\[
\theta=\frac{2\pi n}{13},\qquad \zeta=e^{i\theta}.
\]
Then
\[
\zeta^{13}=e^{13i\theta}=e^{2\pi i n}=1.
\]
Moreover, \(\zeta\ne1\). Indeed, if \(e^{i\theta}=1\), then \(\theta\) would be an integral multiple of \(2\pi\). Thus \(2\pi n/13=2\pi m\) for some integer \(m\), so \(n=13m\), which is impossible for \(1\le n\le12\).

The geometric-series identity gives
\[
(\zeta-1)(1+\zeta+\zeta^2+\cdots+\zeta^{12})=\zeta^{13}-1=0.
\]
Since \(\zeta\ne1\), it follows that
\[
1+\zeta+\zeta^2+\cdots+\zeta^{12}=0. \tag{2}
\]
Also, because \(\zeta=e^{i\theta}\), Euler's formula yields
\[
\zeta+\zeta^{-1}=e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}=2\cos\theta. \tag{3}
\]
The following purely algebraic identity is the key link between the geometric sum and \(g\): for every nonzero complex number \(z\),
\[
z^6g(z+z^{-1})=1+z+z^2+\cdots+z^{12}. \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, substituting the definition of \(g\) into the left side gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
z^6\bigl(&(z+z^{-1})^6+(z+z^{-1})^5-5(z+z^{-1})^4\\
&-4(z+z^{-1})^3+6(z+z^{-1})^2+3(z+z^{-1})-1\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
and expansion and collection of like powers of \(z\) gives exactly
\(z^{12}+z^{11}+\cdots+z+1\), proving (4).

Apply (4) with \(z=\zeta\). By (2), its right side is zero. Since \(\zeta\ne0\), we may cancel \(\zeta^6\), obtaining
\[
g(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})=0.
\]
Using (3) proves (1).

We now introduce the six numbers that occur in the desired factorization:
\[
c_k=4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right),\qquad 1\le k\le6.
\]
The double-angle formula \(\cos(2u)=2\cos^2u-1\) gives
\[
2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{13}\right)
=4\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)-2
=c_k-2. \tag{5}
\]
Taking \(n=k\) in (1) and using (5), we get
\[
g(c_k-2)=0. \tag{6}
\]
A direct expansion of the shift in (6) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
g(t-2)
&=(t-2)^6+(t-2)^5-5(t-2)^4-4(t-2)^3\\
&\qquad+6(t-2)^2+3(t-2)-1\\
&=t^6-11t^5+45t^4-84t^3+70t^2-21t+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently every \(c_k\), \(1\le k\le6\), satisfies
\[
c_k^6-11c_k^5+45c_k^4-84c_k^3+70c_k^2-21c_k+1=0. \tag{7}
\]
Notice that the polynomial in (7) is the reciprocal polynomial of \(P\): for nonzero \(t\),
\[
t^6P(t^{-1})
=t^6-11t^5+45t^4-84t^3+70t^2-21t+1. \tag{8}
\]
Each \(c_k\) is nonzero. In fact,
\[
0<\frac{\pi k}{13}\le\frac{6\pi}{13}<\frac{\pi}{2},
\]
so \(\cos(\pi k/13)>0\), and hence \(c_k>0\). Dividing (7) by \(c_k^6\), or equivalently using (8), gives
\[
P(c_k^{-1})=0 \qquad (1\le k\le6). \tag{9}
\]

We also need these six roots to be distinct. Suppose \(c_i=c_j\) for some \(1\le i,j\le6\). Then
\[
\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi i}{13}\right)
=\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi j}{13}\right).
\]
Both cosines are positive by the preceding angle bounds, so equality of their squares implies
\[
\cos\left(\frac{\pi i}{13}\right)
=\cos\left(\frac{\pi j}{13}\right).
\]
Cosine is injective on \([0,\pi]\) (indeed, it is strictly decreasing there), and both angles lie in this interval. Hence
\[
\frac{\pi i}{13}=\frac{\pi j}{13},
\]
so \(i=j\). Thus the \(c_k\) are pairwise distinct, and because they are nonzero, their reciprocals \(c_k^{-1}\) are pairwise distinct as well.

Consider the monic degree-six polynomial
\[
F(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}(x-c_k^{-1}).
\]
The polynomial \(P\) is also monic of degree six. By (9), both \(P\) and \(F\) vanish at each of the six distinct numbers
\[
c_1^{-1},c_2^{-1},\ldots,c_6^{-1}.
\]
We claim that \(P=F\). If not, \(P-F\) would be a nonzero polynomial. Its degree would be at most five because the leading terms \(x^6\) of the two monic degree-six polynomials cancel. On the other hand, \(P-F\) would vanish at all six of the distinct numbers above. This is impossible, since a nonzero polynomial of degree at most five over \(\mathbb R\) has at most five distinct roots. Therefore
\[
P(x)=F(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}(x-c_k^{-1}). \tag{10}
\]

It remains to convert the monic factorization (10) into the desired factorization, whose factors have constant term one. Evaluating (10) at \(x=0\) and using \(P(0)=1\) gives
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{6}(-c_k^{-1})=1. \tag{11}
\]
Let
\[
A=\prod_{k=1}^{6}(-c_k).
\]
Because every \(c_k\ne0\), multiplication term by term shows
\[
A\prod_{k=1}^{6}(-c_k^{-1})
=\prod_{k=1}^{6}\bigl((-c_k)(-c_k^{-1})\bigr)
=1.
\]
Together with (11), this implies \(A=1\). Finally, for each \(k\),
\[
1-c_kx=-c_k(x-c_k^{-1}).
\]
Multiplying these six identities and using \(A=1\) and (10), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}(1-c_kx)
&=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{6}(-c_k)\right)
  \left(\prod_{k=1}^{6}(x-c_k^{-1})\right)\\
&=A F(x)=P(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting the definition of \(c_k\) gives precisely
\[
1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6
=\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right),
\]
which is the claimed factorization of the denominator.
